extracted.intended_audience: law professors, patent scholars, patent litigators, and judges interested in claim construction doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and doctrinal criteria for interpreting patent claim language (weighting dictionaries, specification, prosecution history, and policy considerations) used by courts, the PTO, and scholars when construing claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weight of linguistic meaning versus purpose of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim terms should be interpreted primarily by their ordinary linguistic meaning (as the Phillips majority favored) or by reference to the purpose/invention (as the dissent favored).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority gives great weight to linguistic considerations and little weight to the purpose of the invention, while the dissent does the opposite; courts sometimes treat purpose as 'lip service' rather than a controlling factor (Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1324-27; Lourie, J., concurring/dissenting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dictionaries versus specification as interpretative aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over reliance on dictionary/extrinsic sources versus using the patent specification (intrinsic evidence) to determine ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars describe a split between the dictionary-dependent and specification-dependent factions; courts have variously quoted dictionaries but also emphasized context from the specification (see citations to Phillips; Mullally; Osenga).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as 'always highly relevant' to claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification contains a written description of the invention and is always highly relevant to the claim construction analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Vitronics: 'The specification contains a written description of the invention . . . . Thus, the specification is always highly relevant to the claim construction analysis.' Courts repeatedly rely on the specification in construing claims (Vitronics, 90 F.3d at 1582).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning must be discerned from intrinsic record context
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ordinary and customary meaning' of a claim term is to be discerned by reference to the context of the intrinsic record (not solely by extrinsic sources like dictionaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nystrom holding: the ordinary meaning must be discerned by reference to the context of the intrinsic record and not by reference to a dictionary, treatise, or other extrinsic source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed through the eyes of a person having ordinary skill in the relevant field, who reads the patent documents with an understanding of their meaning in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiform Desiccants: courts start by reviewing the same resources as PHOSITA—specification and prosecution history; the PHOSITA standard is the central lens for claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history may provide relevant linguistic context
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not physically attached to the claims like the specification, prosecution history can in some circumstances provide relevant linguistic context for claim meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Liebel-Flarsheim (patentee deleted words during prosecution suggesting claims do not include that subject matter). Use prosecution history when it contains clear statements bearing on meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO standard during examination: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO examiners are instructed to adopt a 'broadest reasonable interpretation' when approaching claim language during prosecution to guard against patentee tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Yamamoto, 740 F.2d 1569, 1571 (Fed. Cir. 1984). The PTO historically construes claims more broadly during prosecution than courts do in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory conditions for obtaining a patent (101-103, 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability and claim drafting must satisfy statutory requirements under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101-103, 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections outline subject matter eligibility, novelty/non-obviousness, and written description/enablement/definiteness requirements that bear on claim scope and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency standard as a normative paradigm for determining scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining patent scope is guided by an 'efficiency standard' balancing incentives for innovation against avoidance of monopolies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (Bonito Boats; Merges & Nelson) frame claim scope as an economic-policy tradeoff; some scholars urge policy-informed construction when textual methods are inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ambiguity and vagueness and their interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate linguistic ambiguity (multiple discrete meanings) from vagueness (indeterminate boundaries); legal uncertainty is not identical to linguistic uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vagueness cannot be solved by better interpretative tools; literature conflates vagueness and generality but they are distinct. Example: a claim to 'everything' is not vague even if broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee use of ambiguous language as a strategic tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees may intentionally use ambiguous claim language to pursue 'two-faced' arguments (e.g., broad in court, narrow in prosecution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish deliberate ambiguity (strategic drafting) from invoking ambiguous case law; the problem's severity depends on PTO competency and incentives (Bessen & Meurer; Burk & Lemley).

rubrics_metrics.name: When textual methods yield indeterminate results, policy considerations may inform construction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Phillips methodology does not yield a clear interpretation, courts may consider policy aimed at promoting technological progress to inform claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (Lee; Burk & Lemley) suggest using policy arguments to resolve interpretive indeterminacy rather than relying solely on textualist tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of dictionaries and other extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence like dictionaries can be quoted, but their use is constrained by the context of the intrinsic record and the PHOSITA perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts differ; reliance on dictionaries without intrinsic context is criticized. Phillips and later cases articulate careful, contextualized use of extrinsic sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents is rarely used to find non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has been reluctant to affirm findings of non-infringement under the reverse doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roche Palo Alto v. Apotex notes the court 'has never affirmed a finding of non-infringement under the reverse doctrine of equivalents.' This limits use of that doctrine in narrowing claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators (reversal rates) as evidence of interpretive uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: High reversal rates on claim construction at the Federal Circuit are cited as evidence that claim interpretation is uncertain and contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some scholars argue for expedited appeal or institutional reforms because perceived high reversal rates indicate difficulty in reliable claim construction (Moore; Priest & Klein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Most construed terms are non-technical; technicality is not assumed
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observation that most terms the court construes are not technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Osenga notes many construed terms are ordinary English rather than technical jargon, affecting how courts approach their meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technical advisors or special masters for complex claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may appoint technical advisors or special masters to assist with technological determinations in claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TechSearch v. Intel and studies (Kesan & Ball) support the use of special masters or technical assistance in complex patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation should rely on ordinary English usage conventions as linguistic context (not invention-centered reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification and general subject matter of the patent can provide ordinary-language context (e.g., 'inventory' likely means physical objects) but this is distinct from defining claims by the patentee's inventive contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue for inferring meaning from ordinary usage/context rather than restricting meaning to the patentee's conception of the invention (discussion of 'inventory' examples; Winans v. Denmead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as the best evidence of what ideas the patentee intends to convey
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim language is the best evidence of the patentee's communicated ideas; one should not require knowledge of the inventor's idea before interpreting the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of invention-centered approaches: to say one must know the idea before understanding language is conceptually backward; language should be interpreted on its terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive plurality: methodological splits and judicial choice of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a substantial split in methodological approach among judges and scholars (textualist vs. pragmatic/invention-centered), and judges may choose interpretive methods for normative reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations that judicial decisions reveal more about judge's preferences than about a single correct methodology (Volokh; Wagner & Petherbridge empirical work).
